prompt: Inside the kind node, why does `localhost:5000` not reach the registry without extra configuration?

choices.text: The registry refuses connections from containers
choices.why: It answers anybody who reaches it; the problem is the address.

choices.text: It points at the container it is typed in
choices.why: Right. The node is a container of its own, so its `localhost` is itself, not your machine.

choices.text: containerd only pulls over HTTPS
choices.why: containerd pulls over HTTP when `hosts.toml` says so, which is what the fix does.

choices.text: Kubernetes forbids image names that contain a port
choices.why: `localhost:5000/linkbox:main` is a valid name; the manifest uses it.

prompt: Put the steps that let the kind node pull `localhost:5000/linkbox:main` in order.
items: create the cluster with containerd reading certs.d
make the certs.d directory for localhost:5000 in the node
connect the registry container to the kind network

prompt: Why does the lesson keep the image named `localhost:5000/linkbox:main` in the cluster rather than renaming it `registry:5000/...`?

choices.text: One name everywhere
choices.why: Right. Only the node knows where the name points; everything else, the admission rule included, sees one name.

choices.text: Because `registry` is not a valid host name
choices.why: It is valid on the kind network; the choice is about consistency.

choices.text: Because a rename would need the image rebuilt
choices.why: A tag is a name; it costs no rebuild. The reason is elsewhere.

choices.text: So the image is pulled over TLS
choices.why: The pull is plain HTTP either way; the name decides nothing about TLS here.

prompt: The bare pod `probe`, from an image that runs as 65532 and needs no capability, was refused by the restricted profile. Why?

choices.text: The profile reads the pod's spec, which promised nothing
choices.why: Right: it asks for statements, and the pod made none.

choices.text: The profile scanned the image and found a shell
choices.why: The profile never opens the image, and this image has no shell.

choices.text: Bare pods are forbidden in a restricted namespace
choices.why: Bare pods are allowed if their spec meets the profile.

choices.text: The image came from a registry the cluster does not trust
choices.why: Pod Security Admission does not look at registries; that is the lesson's own policy.

prompt: A deploy step in a pipeline runs `kubectl apply -f k8s/` against a restricted namespace and checks only its exit status. The pod template sets no securityContext. What does the pipeline report?

choices.text: Failure, because Pod Security Admission refuses the Deployment
choices.why: It refuses pods, not Deployments; the Deployment is created with a warning.

choices.text: Success, for a service that has no pod
choices.why: Right. Only `kubectl rollout status`, or an admission rule on the Deployment, would make it fail.

choices.text: Success, and the pods run with the default context
choices.why: The pods are refused; none runs at all.

choices.text: A timeout while the scheduler waits
choices.why: Nothing is waiting: the ReplicaSet's create is refused at once and logged as an event.

prompt: Match each Pod Security Admission mode with what it does.

pairs.right: refuses a pod that breaks the profile
lets it in and prints a warning to whoever applied it
lets it in and records it in the audit log

right_distractors: rewrites the pod to meet the profile

prompt: Where does linkbox's token live once the Deployment runs?

choices.text: In `k8s/linkbox.yaml`, base64-encoded
choices.why: The file names the Secret and holds no token; gitleaks would find one there.

choices.text: In a Secret made by `kubectl`, never in a file
choices.why: Right: `kubectl create secret` from random bytes, referenced by name.

choices.text: In the image, as an environment variable set at build
choices.why: The image has no token; lesson 6 moved it to the environment at run time.

choices.text: In the registry, beside the image
choices.why: The registry stores images only.

prompt: Match each field of linkbox's Deployment with what it does.

pairs.right: the kubelet refuses a container whose user is 0
no API token is mounted in the pod

right_distractors: the image is pulled again on every start

prompt: An image declares `USER nonroot` by name, and its Deployment sets `runAsNonRoot: true`. What happens when the pod starts?

choices.text: It runs, since the name says it is not root
choices.why: A name proves nothing to the kubelet; it needs a number to compare with 0.

choices.text: Refused: a name cannot be verified
choices.why: Right. Use a numeric `USER`, or set `runAsUser` in the manifest.

choices.text: It runs as root, because the name is ignored
choices.why: With `runAsNonRoot`, the kubelet never silently runs as root.

choices.text: The admission policy refuses the Deployment
choices.why: The lesson's policy checks the registry and memory; the user is the kubelet's check.

prompt: In the cluster, `/tmp` and `/data` are `emptyDir` volumes. How do they differ from the `tmpfs` mounts of lesson 9's staging?

choices.text: They survive the pod and keep the data
choices.why: An emptyDir is deleted with the pod, like a tmpfs with its container.

choices.text: They are read-only
choices.why: Both are writable; they are the two writable places.

choices.text: They live on the node's disk and carry no `noexec`
choices.why: Right: the mount table showed `/dev/vda` and `ext4`. `medium: Memory` would put them in memory.

choices.text: They belong to root, so the app cannot write them
choices.why: linkbox wrote its database there and answered 201.

prompt: `kubectl create deployment other -n linkbox --image=python:3.13-slim` printed a Warning and then an error. Which component refused it?

choices.text: Pod Security Admission, in the Warning
choices.why: The Warning only warns; it says the pods would be refused.

choices.text: The LimitRange
choices.why: There was no LimitRange yet, and it judges pods, not Deployments.

choices.text: The ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
choices.why: Right: `images come from the registry at localhost:5000 and nowhere else`.

choices.text: The kubelet, when it failed to pull
choices.why: Nothing was stored, so nothing was ever pulled.

prompt: To send an object through admission without storing it, add `--dry-run=___` to the kubectl command.
Why is the policy's `failurePolicy` set to `Fail`?

choices.text: So a check that errors refuses
choices.why: Right: a check that errors must not let things in, lesson 7's fail-closed rule.

choices.text: So refused Deployments are retried later
choices.why: Nothing retries; `Fail` decides what an evaluation error means.

choices.text: So `kubectl` exits with status 1 on a refusal
choices.why: A refusal already exits non-zero; `failurePolicy` is about the policy failing.

choices.text: So the binding applies to every namespace
choices.why: Which namespaces is the binding's selector; this field is unrelated.

prompt: Somebody pushes an image they built on their laptop to `localhost:5000/linkbox:main` by hand. What does the admission policy do when the Deployment rolls it out?

choices.text: Refuses it, because the pipeline did not build it
choices.why: The policy cannot know who built it; it checks the name only.

choices.text: Accepts it: the name starts with `localhost:5000/`
choices.why: Right. A name is not an identity; lesson 14's signatures close that gap.

choices.text: Refuses it, because the tag `main` already exists
choices.why: Tags move; the registry accepts the push and the policy does not look at tags.

choices.text: Scans it with Trivy before accepting
choices.why: Admission runs no scanner; it evaluates expressions over the manifest.

prompt: Which of these can a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy on Deployments see? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the image name of each container
choices.why: Right: the first rule reads it.

choices.text: whether a container declares a memory limit
choices.why: Right: the second rule reads it.

choices.text: the packages inside the image
choices.why: Admission reads the manifest, not the image's contents.

choices.text: the securityContext fields of the pod template
choices.why: Right: they are part of the Deployment object.

choices.text: the connections the process opens at runtime
choices.why: Runtime behaviour is beyond admission; a runtime detector watches that.

prompt: Why does `quota.yaml` live in the home directory and not in linkbox's `k8s/`?

choices.text: Because quotas cannot be applied with `kubectl apply`
choices.why: They were applied with exactly that.

choices.text: The budget is the cluster owner's
choices.why: Right: the application team works inside limits somebody else sets.

choices.text: Because it holds a secret
choices.why: It holds numbers only.

choices.text: Because gitleaks would flag it
choices.why: Nothing in it looks like a secret.

prompt: The quota allows 512Mi of memory limits and each linkbox pod declares 128Mi. How many linkbox pods fit?
After `kubectl set resources ... --limits=memory=512Mi`, the old pod kept running. Why was there no outage?

choices.text: The LimitRange rewrote the limit down to 256Mi
choices.why: A LimitRange fills in a missing limit; one above its maximum is refused, not rewritten.

choices.text: A rollout removes old pods only as new ones start
choices.why: Right: the new pods were refused, so the old one stayed until the undo.

choices.text: The admission policy refused the update
choices.why: The update declares a memory limit, so the policy accepted it.

choices.text: Kubernetes ignores resource changes until a restart
choices.why: It started a new ReplicaSet at once; its pods were what got refused.

prompt: Match each check with where it refuses.

pairs.right: each pod, against the namespace's total

prompt: A Deployment is applied to the linkbox namespace. Put what checks it, and its pods, in the order they run.
items: the ReplicaSet controller creates a pod
the LimitRange fills in and bounds the pod's limits
the ResourceQuota checks the namespace total
the kubelet checks runAsNonRoot as the container starts
